title: Gas mileage suddenly worse
h1: Why did my gas mileage suddenly get worse?
metaDesc: Gas mileage dropped? Answer a few questions to see if it's tires, weather, a sensor, a dragging brake or an engine problem, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: car using more gas than usual
why is my car using so much gas
intro: Lower fuel economy often has a simple cause, like cold weather or low tires. A sudden drop that comes with other signs can point to a dragging brake, a fuel leak or an engine problem that will get worse. Answer a few questions to see which applies to you.
safety: If you smell raw fuel, stop driving, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and keep sparks and flames away.
If the check engine light is flashing, or the engine shakes, pull over and stop. Driving on can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.
If a wheel is smoking or gives off a strong burning smell, pull over and let it cool.

q_signs.q: Along with the worse mileage, do you notice any of these?
q_signs.help: These signs change how urgent it is, so pick the most serious one that applies.

opts.a: A flashing check engine light, or the engine shaking or misfiring
A smell of raw gasoline, inside or outside the car
A burning smell from a wheel, or the car feels held back, like the brakes are on
The check engine light is on steadily (not flashing)

q_pattern.help: For an accurate number, fill the tank, reset the trip meter, drive normally, then divide the miles driven by the gallons it takes to refill. Dash readouts can be off.

opts.a: It started when the weather turned cold, or I'm making more short trips
The tires look low, or the tire pressure light has come on
Something changed: new tires, a roof rack, towing, a heavier load or a different fuel
The temperature gauge reads lower than usual, or the heater is slow to warm up
The engine feels sluggish, hesitates or idles rough
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring, which wastes fuel and can damage the exhaust
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed, or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't count on it. The misfire may come back, so have it checked before driving further.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the car, step away from it. An overheated catalytic converter can get extremely hot.
If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly. Unburned fuel goes out the exhaust, which is why mileage drops, and it can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter. Stopping early can prevent a much bigger repair.

causes.name: Worn spark plug or failed ignition coil
causes.clues: Shaking at idle or when accelerating, or plugs overdue for replacement.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: The misfire is in one cylinder, or the exhaust smells of fuel.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or mechanical engine problem
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or misfires in several cylinders at once.

you: Note when the light flashes: at idle, when accelerating or when cruising.
shop: Spark plug and ignition coil check

result.title: A fuel leak may be causing both the smell and the lost mileage
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and keep flames and sparks away. Look for wet spots or drips under the car, then have it towed.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move away from the car and call for help.

If the smell was only near the gas cap right after filling up and is now completely gone, a loose or damaged cap is possible. Tighten it, but let a shop confirm that's all it is before relying on the car.
result.why: You should never smell raw gasoline strongly around a car. A leaking fuel line, injector seal or tank can waste fuel quickly, which shows up as worse mileage, and it's a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car, and the smell is strongest outside.

causes.name: Leaking injector or fuel rail seal
causes.clues: The smell is strongest under the hood after driving.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank or filler neck
causes.clues: Wet spots or a smell near the rear of the car.

causes.name: Loose or damaged gas cap
causes.clues: The smell is near the fuel door, and the check engine light may be on.
causes.against: A loose cap alone rarely makes a big difference to mileage.

you: Without starting the engine, look for wet spots or drips under the car.
Check that the gas cap is tight.

result.title: A brake may not be releasing and could be dragging the car
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, make sure the parking brake is fully released, and let the brakes cool. Don't drive it until the brakes have been checked. A brake that keeps dragging can overheat and lose stopping power. A tow, or a mechanic who comes to you, is the safest option.
if: If a wheel is smoking or too hot to go near, keep everyone away from it until it cools. If the smoke gets thicker or doesn't stop, or you think the car may be on fire, call 911, even if you can't see flames.
If the car pulls to one side, the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the brake warning light is on, don't drive it.
If the parking brake was partly on and releasing it stops the drag, the brakes may still have been overheated. Have them checked before relying on them.
result.why: A brake caliper or parking brake that doesn't fully release keeps rubbing, which wastes fuel and creates heat. Left alone, it can overheat the brakes, wear them out fast and weaken your stopping power.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter than the others, has more brake dust, or the car pulls to one side.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully releasing
causes.clues: The brake warning light stays on, or the rear wheels get hot.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: One wheel keeps dragging for a while after you brake.

you: Check that the parking brake is fully off.
After a drive, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to feel if one is much hotter than the others.

result.title: A sensor or engine fault may be making the engine use extra fuel
result.now: Have the trouble codes read. Many auto parts stores offer this, and the code points to the system to test. It doesn't by itself prove which part has failed.
if: If the light starts flashing or the engine runs rough, pull over and stop.
If the gas cap was loose, tighten it. The light may go off on its own after several days of driving.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: The engine computer uses sensors to decide how much fuel to add. When one reads wrong, the engine can run rich (with too much fuel), which costs mileage, and the computer usually turns on the check engine light. The code tells you where to start.

causes.name: Faulty oxygen sensor
causes.clues: Oxygen sensor codes, or mileage that dropped over weeks.

causes.name: Dirty or faulty airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation, rough idle, or airflow sensor codes.

causes.name: Coolant temperature sensor or thermostat
causes.clues: The temperature gauge reads low, or the heater is slow to warm up.

causes.name: Evaporative system leak, like a loose gas cap
causes.clues: Evap codes.
causes.against: This turns the light on but usually doesn't change mileage much.

you: Check that the gas cap is tight.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: Cold weather and short trips may be the main reason
result.now: Check your tire pressure, since cold weather lowers it, and combine short errands into one trip where you can.
if: If mileage doesn't recover when the weather warms up, look for another cause.
If the temperature gauge stays lower than usual even after a long drive, the thermostat may be stuck open.
result.why: Engines use more fuel until they warm up, and in cold weather that takes longer. Winter-blend gasoline holds slightly less energy, cold air and low tire pressure add drag, and the heater, defroster and seat heaters add load. On short trips the engine spends most of its time cold.

causes.name: Cold engine and short trips
causes.clues: Lots of short drives, especially on cold mornings.

causes.name: Lower tire pressure in cold weather
causes.clues: The tire pressure light comes on during cold mornings.

causes.name: Winter-blend fuel and more heater and defroster use
causes.clues: The drop started in late fall and is similar every year.

causes.name: Long warm-up idling
causes.clues: You let the car idle for several minutes before driving.

you: Track mileage by hand over a few full tanks.
Check tire pressure at least monthly in cold weather.
shop: Thermostat and coolant temperature check if the gauge reads low

result.title: Low tire pressure may be costing you fuel
result.now: Check all four tires with a gauge when they're cold, and fill them to the pressure on the sticker inside the driver's door.
if: If one tire keeps losing air, have it checked for a puncture or a leaking valve.
If the tire pressure light stays on after filling, have the tires and their sensors checked.
If a tire is very low, bulging or damaged, don't drive on it. Use the spare or call for help.
result.why: Underinflated tires flex more and roll with more resistance, so the engine works harder to keep the car moving. They also wear faster and grip less. It's the easiest mileage problem to fix.

causes.name: Normal air loss over time
causes.clues: All four tires are a little low.

causes.name: Cold weather
causes.clues: The light comes on during cold mornings.

causes.name: Puncture or leaking valve
causes.clues: One tire is much lower than the others.

you: Check pressure with a gauge, not by eye.
Use the pressure on the door sticker, not the maximum printed on the tire.

result.title: A recent change may be the reason
result.now: Think about what changed around the time the mileage dropped, and undo it where you can, like removing an empty roof rack or extra weight.
if: If you switched to fuel with more ethanol, lower mileage is expected. Only use fuels your owner's manual approves.
If the drop came right after new tires, check their pressure. Some tires simply roll with more resistance.
If the drop came right after a repair, mention it to the shop that did the work.
result.why: Fuel economy depends on how hard the engine has to work. Extra weight, towing, roof racks and cargo boxes add load or wind drag, and tires with more grip or a different size can roll harder. Fuel with more ethanol holds less energy per gallon.

causes.name: Roof rack, cargo box, towing or extra weight
causes.clues: The drop appeared right after you added it.

causes.name: New tires
causes.clues: A different type or size, or they're underinflated.

causes.name: Fuel with more ethanol
causes.clues: You switched stations or fuel types.

causes.name: A change in how or where you drive
causes.clues: More fast highway driving, or more stop-and-go traffic.

you: Remove unneeded weight and racks, then track the next tank.
shop: Tire and alignment check if the drop came with new tires

result.title: The thermostat may be stuck open, so the engine never fully warms up
result.now: Watch where the temperature gauge settles on your next longer drive, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the gauge ever climbs toward hot, pull over and turn the engine off. That's a different and more serious problem.
If the heater barely warms the cabin in winter, get it checked sooner, because the defroster may not clear the windshield.
result.why: The thermostat keeps coolant in the engine until it warms up. If it sticks open, the engine runs cooler than it should. The engine computer then adds extra fuel as if the engine were still cold, which lowers mileage.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: The gauge sits low on the highway, and the heater is lukewarm.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: A check engine light, or the gauge acting oddly.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The coolant reservoir is low, and the heater blows cool air at times.

you: Note where the gauge settles after a 15-minute drive.
Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.

result.title: An engine performance problem may be making it work harder
result.now: Have the engine checked in the next few days, including a code scan even if the check engine light isn't on.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the car struggles badly uphill or the exhaust smells like rotten eggs, a blocked catalytic converter is possible. Get it checked sooner.
If you smell raw fuel, see smoke, or smell burning from under the car, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: An engine that's down on power has to work harder to do the same job, so it uses more fuel. Worn spark plugs, a dirty airflow sensor or a partly blocked exhaust are common reasons, and they usually get worse over time.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or a weak ignition coil
causes.clues: Plugs overdue for replacement, hesitation, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Dirty airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation, surging or a rough idle.

causes.name: Restricted catalytic converter
causes.clues: Sluggish mostly uphill or at highway speed, a rotten egg smell, or a rattle underneath.

causes.name: Clogged air filter
causes.clues: The filter is visibly dirty.
causes.against: On modern fuel-injected cars a dirty filter mostly hurts acceleration, not mileage.

you: Note when it hesitates: cold, warm, uphill or at idle.
Check your service records for when the spark plugs were last changed.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: Confirm the drop over a tank or two, then have the basics checked
result.now: Check tire pressure, then measure your mileage by hand over the next full tank to confirm the drop.
if: If the drop is large and sudden, or another symptom shows up, have it checked sooner.
If the check engine light comes on, get the codes read.
If you smell raw fuel or burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it checked first.
result.why: Mileage naturally varies with weather, traffic, fuel and driving style, and dash readouts can be off. A measured drop that sticks around usually comes from tires, brakes, sensors or engine wear, and a shop can check those quickly.

causes.name: Tire pressure or wheel alignment
causes.clues: Tires look low, or uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Changes in driving or weather
causes.clues: More short trips, more traffic, or colder weather.

causes.name: Sensor or engine problem not yet setting a warning light
causes.clues: The engine feels slightly less lively.

causes.name: Slightly dragging brake
causes.clues: One wheel has more brake dust or feels warmer.

you: Measure mileage by hand over a full tank.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data
